Aftab et al.: The Standardized Soil Moisture-Temperature Compound Index (SSTCI) Introduction Climate extremes are increasingly disrupting societies and ecosystems, with anthropogenic warming driving more frequent and intense heatwaves and droughts across many regions (Seneviratne and Zhang, 2021). When these hazards co-occur, their combined impacts are disproportionately severe relative to either stressor alone (Miralles et al., 2014; Zscheischler et al., 2018). Historic cases clearly emphasize these escalating risks, including Europe’s Mega-heatwave summers (2003, 2010), which led to excess mortality and agricultural losses (Barriopedro et al., 2011); and concurrent dry-hot (DH) conditions, which were linked to substantial crop impacts, including ∼ 20 % reductions in U.S. corn area affected by concurrent extremes and ∼ 25 % national production loss in Russia in 2010–2011 (Feng et al., 2019; Barriopedro et al., 2011). More recently, the prolonged compound dry-hot extreme (CDHE) event of 2022 in the Yangtze River basin led to widespread heatstroke, forest fires, and a reduction in lake size (Lu et al., 2023; Lu et al., 2024). To better understand such extremes, a substantial body of work has developed diagnostic approaches spanning process based and statistical perspectives (Sabut and Mishra, 2026). Process oriented studies have characterized the soil moisture–temperature coupling that underlies compound dry-hot conditions (Miralles et al., 2012), showing how soil desiccation and atmospheric heat accumulation combine to produce mega-heatwaves (Miralles et al., 2012, 2014). In parallel, multivariate statistical approaches have been explored to quantify compound conditions directly. Among these, the copula function has proven particularly effective in capturing complex dependencies between climate variables, enabling the construction of joint distributions that integrate multiple indi

in the water, energy and carbon cycles, modulating the surface energy balance (Osman et al., 2022; Seneviratne et al., 2010). When precipitation deficits deplete SM, reduced evapotranspiration causes a larger share of surface net radiation to be partitioned into sensible heat flux, thereby enhancing nearsurface warming. (Tabari and Willems, 2023). This shift can accelerate the onset and increase the intensity of hot extremes (Seo and Ha, 2022). Furthermore, such land–atmosphere feedback can be critical even in regions that are typically humid. For example, analyses of the 2022 heatwave in the Yangtze River basin, China, showed that its exceptional severity was linked to a transition from an energy-limited to a water-limited coupling regime under extremely low soil moisture conditions (Ni et al., 2024). Focusing on this evolving land–atmosphere feedback is therefore essential for understanding the persistence and intensity of CDHEs. Soil moisture widely used and provide direct measures of surface moisture conditions, however many of the standardized drought indices adopted to compute compound indices remain precipitation driven, such as the Standardized Precipitation Index (Liu et al., 2024), the Standardized Precipitation– Evapotranspiration Index (Vicente-Serrano et al., 2010), the Palmer Drought Severity Index (Zhong et al., 2019), and the Standardized antecedent precipitation evaporation index (Li et al., 2020).This meteorological focus yields an indirect view that overlooks direct soil conditions and the vital antecedent SM memory (McColl et al., 2017), leading to an insufficient assessment of actual ecosystem water stress. Working directly with soil moisture is necessary but not sufficient, since the coupling is driven by accumulated antecedent depletion rather than by the moisture state on any single day. An instantaneous standardized soil moisture index describes a snapshot and omits the progressive dry-down through which https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-18-7981-2026 R. Aftab et al.: The Standardized Soil Moisture-Temperature Compound Index (SSTCI) soil moisture modulates temperature, and the timescale over which that depletion accumulates varies widely between fast drying semi-arid and slowly buffered humid environments (McColl et al., 2017; Rahmati et al., 2024). A soil moisture centric compound index therefore requires both a direct soil moisture state variable and a location specific representation of its memory along with temperature extremes. Consequently, a continuous, consistent global daily scale index is needed to capture the swift onset, intensification, and decay dynamics characteristic of CDHEs. In this study, we present the Standardized Soil Moisture Temperature Compound Index (SSTCI), a global, daily (0.1° × 0.1°) dataset from 1961–2023. SSTCI integrates a standardized antecedent soil moisture index (SASMI), calculated with grid specific dry down memory of

s, end dates, durations, and severity metrics for every compound event detected globally over the last 63 years. This paper offers a comprehensive overview of the datasets and methodologies employed, outlined in Sect. 2. Section 3 provides an in-depth analysis of the results, including the global event characteristics and case studies, coupled with a detailed discussion, and closes with limitations and outlook (Sect. 3.9). Section 4 delivers a concise conclusion, and the availability of the developed datasets is covered in Sect. 5 2 Data and Methods 2.1 Data sources This study utilizes global reanalysis datasets from the Copernicus Climate Data Store to calculate SSTCI. Volumetric soil water content in the uppermost soil layer (0–7 cm; variable swvl1) is taken from the ERA5-Land, land-surface reanalysis at 0.1° spatial resolution (Muñoz-Sabater et al., 2021). Given the lack of a long, spatially consistent in situ soil-moisture observing network at the global scale, we adopt ERA5-Land soil moisture for this analysis. https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-18-7981-2026 7983 ERA5-Land provides multi-decadal, globally complete hourly fields and has been shown to realistically capture surface soil moisture variability and anomalies across a wide range of hydroclimatic regimes when evaluated against large in situ networks (Hagan et al., 2020; Beck et al., 2021). The 0–7 cm layer is used because SSTCI targets the dailyscale onset and evolution of compound dry-hot conditions, for which the near-surface layer is where land–atmosphere coupling is most directly expressed: it controls direct soil evaporation and is most tightly tied to the daytime surface energy balance that governs latent–sensibl

f conditions driving dryhot events. Antarctica is excluded due to persistent snow/ice, and all ocean grid cells are masked. We additionally used four independent datasets for evaluation.
